However, further improvements to the battery storage solution might be obtained through SCM—leveraging temporally flexible loads—to increase savings and reduce investments in distributed energy resources (DER), which include BESS and solar photovoltaics (PV). 2 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2 Load Management Solutions Load growth could increase demand charges, consume energy during peak pricing windows, and trigger site or grid equipment upgrades. However, coordination between DER assets, load monitoring, and management can support significant cost savings. The Athena team has developed tools to forecast load growth, site capacity limitations, utility rates, and EV charging operations to size DER solutions with load management potential. These resources are designed to help airports estimate system requirements and ensure new loads are supported by the appropriate solutions, minimizing costs and optimizing site operation. 2.1 Scoping Generation and Storage Needs Athena used NLR’s Enabling Distributed Generation Energy Storage (EDGES) model to generate optimal BESS design solutions presented in the Aeroportal [9]. EDGES employs a bi- level optimization approach, coupled with high-fidelity simulation and accurate financial modeling, to identify the DER configuration—BESS and PV—or required grid distribution upgrades that minimize the project’s life cycle costs [10]. While SCM strategies are not directly supported by EDGES (the load profile is provided as a fixed time series), DER solutions obtained with this tool were used to inform the initial configurations to be tested against the site controllers described in this work and within the emulation environment described in Section 3.2. 2.2 Leveraging Load Flexibility EV charging loads are based on several factors that are a function of the vehicle and EVSE hardware—for example, the battery pack temperature and maximum charge voltage and current. A large fleet of vehicles, if left unmanaged, could quickly exceed the site’s electrical capacity from the utility. The most common result of this high peak demand is an overloaded transformer or an overengineered utility connection that is more costly than necessary. Due to the nature of vehicle dwell time, rental fleets have some flexibility that can be leveraged by an SCM controller. For example, utilizing several EVSE with diverse power levels such as 350 kW down to 20 kW allows the fleet to prioritize high-demand vehicles at the higher-power chargers while pushing the lower-demand vehicles to the lower-power chargers. Each vehicle will hit its target SOC by the time it is scheduled to depart, but not every vehicle needs to charge at the maximum rate. This allows for a more optimized load profile across the site that could mitigate costly bills or upgrades as a result of demand charges or overloaded equipment.
